newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan government listens to rights groups.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan government listens to rights groups.

text.p: The Venezuelan government held a ground-breaking first meeting with non-government and human rights organisations on Friday in an effort to improve an often testy debate over rights abuses.
The all-day seminar brought together top government officials and representatives from about 40 groups to discuss an agenda to improve the country's rights record.

"We haven't come here to argue or make controversy between different points of view but rather to try to bring together these points of view," President Rafael Caldera said in an opening address to the conference.
He did not stay to talk with the rights groups, something he has not done since he came to power in February 1994.
"We have asked for interviews with the president regularly during these past years but we are always told he is too busy to talk to us," Raul Cubas, director of local rights group Provea, said.

But other government officials said they welcomed the opportunity to exchange opinions. "I've come here to listen. I'm sure we're going to receive a lot of criticism," National Prisons Director Monica Fernandez said.
Venezuela's overcrowded and violent jails, where inmates spend an average of four years awaiting sentence, receive the brunt of criticism from international human rights groups.

"We've managed to reduce violent incidents but it's still not enough," Fernandez said. She added that her department was trying to educate guards accustomed to beating inmates and charging them for food and rides to court.

At a series of roundtable meetings on Friday, government officials were to give their views on a document presented by rights groups containing more than 400 proposals to improve human rights in Venezuela.
"This is a first step towards ordering the government's approach to human rights," Alvaro Briceno, head of Amnesty International in Venezuela, said.
The proposals included moves to stamp out the use of torture by security forces and annulling a vagrants law that rights groups say leads to arbitrary arrests.
